question: What did churned customers say about support and customer success after onboarding?

resolution.read_instruction: Extract every statement the customer makes about OrbitFlow's support and customer success after onboarding, including comments on responsiveness, account management, check-ins, training, escalations, ticket resolution, and any complaints or praise, along with the context of when these issues arose and whether they contributed to the decision to leave.
assumptions: 'Churned customers' maps to the Churn post-mortem call type.
'After onboarding' is interpreted as post-implementation ongoing support and customer success, not the onboarding process itself.
Question asks for customer statements, so the reader should extract the customer's perspective on support and CS.

findings.speaker: Kwame Boateng
findings.quote: We had a two-day onboarding at the start. Eight people attended. Six of them never touched it again.
findings.context: Verity's only post-onboarding enablement was a two-day onboarding at the start, attended by eight people, six of whom never touched the product again. Nothing followed until OrbitFlow's CS offered sessions in January, which Verity declined. — Post-onboarding gap in CS follow-through; the January offer came about a year after the initial onboarding and after the customer had already half-concluded the product would not work.

findings.speaker: Kwame Boateng
findings.quote: Nothing, until you arrived in January and offered some sessions.
findings.context: Verity's head of operations said the January sessions OrbitFlow offered were not what would have helped; he said they had nothing hands-on from OrbitFlow until the January offer. — Customer's account of what was missing; he declined the January offer because the team's time was not worth spending by then.

findings.speaker: Kwame Boateng
findings.quote: if someone had sat with two of my people for a week in the first quarter and got them to ship something real, we'd still be a customer.
findings.context: The customer said that hands-on help in the first quarter, sitting with two of their people and shipping a real workflow, would have kept them as a customer. — Customer's view of the CS intervention that would have changed the outcome; contrasts with the generic training and sessions they were offered.

findings.speaker: Kwame Boateng
findings.quote: Do you? Nobody ever offered it to me.
findings.context: OrbitFlow's hands-on build engagement (sitting with the team to build workflows) is a paid professional services add-on, and the customer said nobody had ever offered it to them. — Vendor confirmed the service is paid; customer said it was never offered during their tenure, and the vendor said the paid-add-on model may be the problem.

findings.speaker: Sarah Lindqvist
findings.quote: The support was inconsistent. Some tickets came back in an hour with someone who clearly understood the product. Others came back in a day with a link to documentation I'd already read and cited in the ticket.
findings.context: Support response quality was inconsistent: some tickets were answered within an hour by knowledgeable staff, while others took a day and returned only documentation the customer had already read. — Customer described this as a grievance that was not the reason they left, but it fed a sense of being a small account. Vendor attributed it to a triage problem.

findings.speaker: Sarah Lindqvist
findings.quote: But it contributed to a general feeling that we were a small account.
findings.context: The support inconsistency was not a stated reason for leaving but contributed to a general feeling that Verity was treated as a small account. — Explicitly contributory rather than causal; the customer separates it from the reason they left.

findings.speaker: Ruth Adeyemi
findings.quote: You were an eighty-thousand-pound account in a book of accounts where that's below median.
findings.context: Verity's engineering manager said the company was probably treated as a small account, and the vendor said it was an eighty-thousand-pound account below the median of its book. — Vendor's own framing of account tiering as the reason for lower-touch service; the customer accepted it.

findings.speaker: Sarah Lindqvist
findings.quote: That was an accurate and completely useless answer.
findings.context: When Verity asked in April for a fix to the connector problem, OrbitFlow's CSM checked for a template, found none, and only emailed that answer. The customer said that answer was accurate but useless, and that the right response would have been hands-on engineering help. — Escalation failure in April 2025-era renewal-risk period, before the Workato PoC; the vendor agreed the answer was useless.

findings.speaker: Ruth Adeyemi
findings.quote: I'd have had to argue for it. I might have lost.
findings.context: The CSM said that giving Verity a solutions-architect engagement at renewal risk would have needed internal argument and might have been refused. — Vendor admission that the escalation resources were not reliably available for at-risk accounts; the vendor said it would raise this internally.

findings.speaker: Kwame Boateng
findings.context: The customer said nothing OrbitFlow could have done in the last six months would have changed the outcome, because the Workato evaluation had already started by March. — Customer view on whether late CS intervention could have saved the account; their earlier statements suggest the earlier hands-on help mattered more.

findings.speaker: Hazel Wren
findings.quote: Fine. Genuinely fine. I think I've raised two tickets in two years and both were answered.
findings.context: Customer says the last year of service was fine and she raised about two support tickets in two years, both answered. — Post-onboarding support experience; praise, low contact volume. Not cited as a reason for leaving.

findings.speaker: Hazel Wren
findings.quote: You did, in — March? An email about a new feature.
findings.context: Customer says OrbitFlow contacted her only once in the period, via a March product announcement email, which she does not count as contact. — Account management / check-ins after onboarding; customer views this as no real CSM contact.

findings.speaker: Hazel Wren
findings.quote: Someone should have noticed after six months that we had four users on a thirty-user plan and said something. Not sold me something. Said something.
findings.context: Customer says no one at OrbitFlow noticed after six months that Oakhill had four users on a thirty-user plan and said something; she wanted someone to raise it, not sell to her. — Account monitoring / proactive CS after onboarding; customer frames it as a missed opportunity that contributed to the eventual churn.

findings.speaker: Hazel Wren
findings.quote: But it does rather answer the question of why nobody noticed the four users.
findings.context: Customer says the lack of attention from OrbitFlow is a plausible explanation for why nobody noticed the low usage. — Customer links the absence of an assigned CSM to the missed usage signal.

findings.speaker: Ruth Adeyemi
findings.quote: Your account was in a segment that doesn't get an assigned CSM. I'm on this call because it's a churn, not because I've been managing you.
findings.context: OrbitFlow staff say Oakhill's account segment does not get an assigned CSM, and the CSM is on the call because it is a churn. — Vendor admission about post-onboarding account management coverage for this customer tier.

findings.speaker: Ruth Adeyemi
findings.quote: We look at it. Whether anyone acts on it for an account your size is a different question, and the answer is usually no.
findings.context: OrbitFlow staff say they look at usage data but acting on it for an account of Oakhill's size is usually not done. — Vendor admission about usage-based proactive outreach after onboarding.

findings.speaker: Alastair McCrae
findings.quote: I probably should have pushed harder on whether you had the capacity for the roadmap we talked about.
findings.context: Vendor account executive says he should have pushed harder on the customer's capacity to run the roadmap, which contributed to the underuse after onboarding. — Sales-side acknowledgement tied to post-sale adoption; not a support complaint but related to post-onboarding success.

findings.speaker: Hazel Wren
findings.quote: I've got no complaint about the product at all.
findings.context: Customer says the real reason she left was the subscription being underused and the problem fading from view, not any support failure; she has no product complaint. — Stated reason for churn is cost versus value; support was not a driver of the decision.

findings.speaker: Ruth Adeyemi
findings.quote: It's not a thing we offer, but it's eleven workflows and it'll take an hour.
findings.context: OrbitFlow staff offered an exit assistance: a custom screenshot export of eleven workflows and a read-only extension to the end of November at no charge, which the customer describes as generous. — Post-churn offboarding support, not ongoing service; vendor described the screenshot export as not a normal offering.

draft.answer: Verity Payments said post-onboarding enablement was thin and that hands-on help in the first quarter would have kept them, and they described inconsistent support that made them feel like a small account [C1][C2][C3]. Oakhill Property called support fine but said OrbitFlow never noticed low usage and had no real CSM contact [C4][C5]. Neither customer's support experience was the stated reason for leaving [C6].

claims.text: Verity's Kwame Boateng said their only enablement was a two-day onboarding (eight attendees, six never touched the product again), and that nothing followed until OrbitFlow's CS offered sessions in January, which Verity declined.

Boateng said that if someone had sat with two of Verity's people for a week in the first quarter and got them to ship something real, they would still be a customer. He said the paid hands-on engagement was never offered to him. He also said that nothing in the last six months would probably have changed the outcome, since the Workato evaluation had started by March.

Verity's Sarah Lindqvist said support was inconsistent: some tickets were answered within an hour by knowledgeable staff, others took a day and returned documentation she had already cited. It was not a reason for leaving but contributed to feeling like a small account; CSM Ruth Adeyemi framed Verity as an £80k account below the median of the book.

When Verity asked in April for a connector fix, the CSM only emailed that no template existed. Lindqvist called this accurate but useless and said hands-on engineering help was needed. Adeyemi admitted a solutions-architect engagement would have needed internal argument and she might have lost.

Oakhill Property's Hazel Wren said support was fine, with about two tickets in two years, both answered. She said OrbitFlow's only contact was a March feature-announcement email, which she did not count as real contact.

Wren said someone should have noticed after six months that Oakhill had four users on a thirty-user plan and said something, not sold to her. Adeyemi confirmed Oakhill's segment gets no assigned CSM and that usage data is looked at but usually not acted on for an account that size. Wren said this explains why nobody noticed. AE Alastair McCrae said he should have pushed harder on capacity for the roadmap.

Wren said her reason for leaving was underuse and the problem fading from view, not a support failure, and that she has no product complaint. Lindqvist likewise separated support issues from the reason Verity left.
OrbitFlow offered Oakhill exit help: a screenshot export of eleven workflows and a read-only extension to the end of November at no charge.

not_covered: Only two churn post-mortem calls (Verity Payments, Oakhill Property) are covered, so this may not represent other churned customers.
